To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
preschoolers' theory-of-mind abilities impact their ability to learn new words from knowledgeable versus un-informed speakers.
preschoolers learn better when speakers are knowledgeable than when they are ignorant, but only when the speaker's ignorance is genuine.
4 year olds, but not 3 year olds consider speakers' knowledge when establishing initial word links, whereas 3 year olds are sensitive to speakers' ignorance, but not knowledge.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how children learn new words.
the question of whether children consider speakers’ knowledge states when establishing word referent links, and if so, when they start doing so.
the role of theory of mind (ToM) in semantic development, and more specifically, with whether preschoolers consider speakers' knowledge about referents when establishing initial word links.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the development of a theory of mind is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for the development of a semantic system.
children's semantic development is linked to their theory of mind.
preschoolers' semantic development is influenced by their theory of mind development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
preschoolers are more likely to learn new words from knowledgeable speakers, and they are more likely to consider speakers' ignorance when they express uncertainty about a word's referent.
children are sensitive to speakers' knowledge states in word learning and this sensitivity is related to their developing theory of mind.
preschoolers consider the speaker's knowledge state in word learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children's word learning is sensitive to the knowledge states of their interlocutors, and that this knowledge is used to inform their word learning.
children's semantic development is linked to the development of their ability to understand other people's knowledge states.
children's theory of mind abilities are important for their word learning.
